analysis.one_liner: Strips the EPA's power to block permits that dump dredged or fill material into waterways.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal the EPA's Clean Water Act veto over dredge-and-fill permits was introduced in January 2011, sent to a House subcommittee, and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the Clean Water Act, the Army Corps of Engineers issues permits allowing companies to dump dredged soil or fill material into rivers, streams, and wetlands. The EPA keeps a final backstop: it can block or restrict a disposal site even after the Corps signs off. This bill would erase that EPA veto power (Section 404(c)), leaving the Corps' permitting decision as the final word. The bill was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then to its Water Resources subcommittee, where it died without any action.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies that want to deposit fill or mine waste into waterways — mining companies, real estate developers, and others seeking dredge-and-fill permits — would benefit, because the EPA could no longer overrule an approved permit or forbid use of a disposal site even after years of agency review.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals Section 404(c) of the Clean Water Act, eliminating the EPA Administrator's authority to prohibit the specification of, or deny or restrict the use of, an area as a disposal site for dredged or fill material [S2, S3].
Removes the possibility that a permit already approved by the Army Corps could later be blocked by the EPA, ending that source of uncertainty for permit applicants [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: People who live downstream of or near permitted dump sites — including communities that depend on rivers, streams, wetlands, and fisheries for drinking water, recreation, and their livelihoods — would lose the last regulatory safeguard that can stop an approved discharge of dredged or fill material into those waters.

drawbacks.text: The EPA's 404(c) authority is the only tool in the Clean Water Act that can stop a dredge-and-fill discharge after the Army Corps has issued a permit; repealing it removes the final check on Corps permitting decisions [S2, S3].

Industry groups and permit holders argue the opposite: the possibility of an EPA veto after a permit is granted creates years-long uncertainty, and the Corps' own permitting review should be sufficient. The bill's design answers this by simply eliminating the EPA's authority rather than adding any substitute safeguard [S2, S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades a single federal backstop for industry convenience. The Army Corps would still review and issue permits, so day-to-day permitting continues; what disappears is the one authority that can reverse a decision after the fact. For companies with large investments at stake, that predictability has real value. For people who drink from, fish in, or live near the affected waters, the cost is the loss of a rarely used but last-resort protection against discharges into the nation's waters. On balance, the bill's benefit flows to permit applicants and its risk falls on the public.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in January 2011 and referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, which sent it to the Water Resources and Environment subcommittee; nothing further ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Don Young of Alaska introduced the bill on January 26, 2011, joined by nine original Republican cosponsors [S3].
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure [S1, S5].
On January 27, 2011, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment, which was the last action the bill ever received [S5].
The 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013, with the bill never having been reported out of committee, scheduled, or voted on [S1, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People who use and depend on the nation's rivers, wetlands, and coastal waters, who keep the EPA's existing authority to block dredge-and-fill dump sites. Permit-seeking companies avoid gaining new leverage.

for.name: Rep. Don Young
for.role: U.S. Representative from Alaska; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal Section 404(c) of the Clean Water Act on January 26, 2011.

for.name: 12 House Republican cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Bishop of Utah, Chaffetz, Jones, McKinley, Carter, Poe of Texas, Broun, Latta, and Griffith of Virginia among the original cosponsors.

against.name: House Water Resources and Environment Subcommittee
against.role: Subcommittee of the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee holding the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 27, 2011 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 cosponsors were Republicans, with no Democratic support recorded [S4].

industries.note: Repealing 404(c) removes the EPA's authority to veto or restrict the use of a site for dumping mine waste or dredged material, a backstop mining projects have most often faced. The cost lands on communities and fisheries downstream of permitted discharges [S2, S3].

industries.industry: Real estate developers and heavy construction
industries.note: Developers filling wetlands and waterways for projects would gain certainty that an approved Corps permit cannot later be revoked by the EPA. The public loses the final safeguard against discharges into those waters [S2, S3].
